title: MTRX™ Field Guide to Sales and Persuasion · 28 days

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: True or false: any emotional appeal is manipulation.
cards.answer: False. Emotion can make a real stake visible. It becomes suspect when emotion replaces evidence, hides the speaker’s motive, or exploits a vulnerability that makes refusal difficult.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: If a client says yes after your explanation, have you proved the pitch was ethical?
cards.answer: No. Consent is not the only test. Ask whether the claim was truthful, the choice was understandable, the risks were visible, and the client could decline without punishment.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: In 60 words: how do persuasion, manipulation and coercion differ?
cards.answer: Persuasion is an open attempt to change judgement or action while leaving the other person able to inspect reasons and refuse. Manipulation hides or exploits the process, motive or vulnerability, often bypassing deliberation. Coercion adds a threat or unacceptable penalty for refusal. The boundaries are debated, so disclose interests and preserve agency.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: What are ethos, pathos and logos?
cards.answer: They are appeals through perceived character and credibility, emotion, and reasoning or evidence. None is automatically ethical or dishonest.

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: What is the Nyaya lesson for a sales call?
cards.answer: Ask whether the conversation seeks shared inquiry, victory or demolition. A pitch that only aims to win can look rational while ignoring fit and correction.

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: What does Han Feizi add?
cards.answer: A correct argument can fail because status, fear, incentives and timing shape whether it is heard. Message quality and relationship risk are separate variables.

cards.name: Is persuasion just manipulation with better manners?
cards.q: You are about to DM a Costa Rican eco-lodge: “Your website is losing bookings, book my $400 retainer this week.” What is the honest rewrite?
cards.answer: Name the observation and its limits: “I noticed the mobile booking path takes four steps after Instagram. I may be missing context. I made a two-minute screen recording showing where a visitor could hesitate. If this is not a priority, no reply is needed. If it is, we can inspect the numbers together before discussing scope.” It uses evidence, relevance and a real exit, not fear.

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: True or false: the best salesperson can sell anything to anyone.
cards.answer: False. Fit, timing, budget, authority and trust constrain a sale. A useful seller disqualifies poor fits instead of treating every no as a persuasion failure.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: Does “always be closing” mean you should ask for the order on every interaction?
cards.answer: No. The next decision may be a diagnostic, access to data, a stakeholder introduction or a date for review. In larger sales, premature closing can interrupt diagnosis.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is selling when done well?
cards.answer: Selling is a structured conversation that helps a plausible buyer understand a problem, compare alternatives, inspect evidence, assess risk and choose a next step. It includes disqualification, not only persuasion. In a service business, delivery, boundaries and proof are part of selling because the buyer is purchasing future reliability, not merely code or a feature list.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: What were NCR’s four Primer stages?
cards.answer: Approach, proposition, demonstration and close, supported by scripts, territory management, training and measurement.

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: Why is “always be closing” a poor universal rule?
cards.answer: A premature close can interrupt discovery. The right next decision might be access, diagnosis, a stakeholder meeting or a calendarised review.

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: What should you measure instead of vague activity?
cards.answer: Positive replies, meetings held, qualified opportunities, proposals, wins, margin, sales cycle, churn and referrals, with clear denominators.

cards.name: What is selling, really?
cards.q: A safari brand replies, “Send your rates.” What should you do before sending three packages?
cards.answer: Give a useful range with scope assumptions, then ask two fit questions: what booking or enquiry outcome matters, and who owns the website or booking system? Offer a short audit if useful. The aim is not to hide price. It is to prevent a generic menu from replacing diagnosis and to make the next decision reversible.

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: True or false: if Cialdini names seven principles, each is a reliable conversion button.
cards.answer: False. They are broad mechanisms with moderators, overlap and failures. Use them as hypotheses, then measure the honest version in the actual context.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: Is a testimonial automatically social proof?
cards.answer: No. It is evidence only if the person is real, the result is relevant and the context is comparable. A pile of vague logos can create noise or suspicion.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: In 60 words: how should a founder use Cialdini’s principles?
cards.answer: Treat each principle as a hypothesis about uncertainty, identity, obligation or credibility. Use only truthful evidence and a voluntary path. Test a relevant norm, a useful contribution or a clear credential against a neutral version, and track qualified outcomes plus opt-outs. If the cue works only by hiding risk or making refusal uncomfortable, remove it.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: What did the hotel study actually support?
cards.answer: A relevant descriptive norm could outperform a generic environmental appeal in that setting. It did not show that social proof always works.

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: What is the ethical difference between reciprocity and a bribe-like gift?
cards.answer: A useful, unsolicited contribution can help without creating debt. A gift designed to make refusal feel impossible exploits obligation and should not be used.

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: What is pre-suasion?
cards.answer: Shaping attention or the frame before the main request. It changes what is salient, not what is true, and should not hide material information.

cards.name: Why do people say yes?
cards.q: You want to send an audit to a lodge prospect. How can you use social proof without fake urgency?
cards.answer: Use one permissioned, comparable case with baseline and outcome: “A 12-room lodge in a similar booking model reduced enquiry steps from four to two in a pilot; here is what was measured and what was not.” Add an easy opt-out. Do not say “most lodges are already doing this” unless you have a defensible, relevant dataset.

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: True or false: a polished portfolio proves trust.
cards.answer: False. It can signal ability, but not reliability, benevolence or integrity. A buyer also needs boundaries, references, process visibility and a credible remedy when something goes wrong.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: If a client likes you personally, is the trust problem solved?
cards.answer: No. Liking may open the door, but service buying involves delivery risk, data risk, price risk and continuity. Convert warmth into inspectable commitments.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: In 60 words: how does a small studio build trust with a distant buyer?
cards.answer: Make hidden quality visible. Show relevant work and the method behind it, state exactly what is included and excluded, identify who will do the work, use permissioned references, stage the commitment, protect data and define a remedy. Warmth helps, but trust grows when ability, benevolence and integrity are repeatedly evidenced under real constraints.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: What are Mayer’s three trustworthiness dimensions?
cards.answer: Ability, benevolence and integrity. They are distinct perceptions, not interchangeable versions of charisma.

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: Why do signals matter in Akerlof’s lemons problem?
cards.answer: They help a buyer infer hidden quality when direct inspection is difficult. Credible signals constrain or expose the seller, rather than merely claiming excellence.

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: What is the safe lesson from Gujarati and diamond trading networks?
cards.answer: Trust can be built through repeated relationships, references, information and sanctions. Do not turn community history into a stereotype or assume insiders are always trustworthy.

cards.name: Why does trust decide the deal?
cards.q: An overseas eco-lodge asks, “Why should we trust an Ahmedabad studio with our booking funnel?” What should you show?
cards.answer: A permissioned, comparable case with baseline and outcome; a short technical audit showing your method; a one-page SOW with response times, ownership and exclusions; staged payment or a bounded pilot; and a clear data and handoff plan. You should say what you do not yet know and invite the buyer to verify a reference. That lowers risk without pretending distance is irrelevant.

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: True or false: ELM says every person has a fixed central or peripheral personality.
cards.answer: False. Route use depends on motivation, ability, relevance, distraction and the message. The same buyer can scrutinise a security promise and skim a font choice.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: If a beautiful website gets attention, has it proved the service works?
cards.answer: No. Attention is an entry condition. Proof of outcomes still needs relevant evidence, and a polished cue can also trigger persuasion knowledge.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: In 60 words: what does ELM actually predict?
cards.answer: ELM predicts that motivation and ability affect the likelihood of elaboration. With high relevance, time and knowledge, argument quality has more influence and attitudes can be durable. With low elaboration, cues such as authority, fluency or consensus matter more. The routes are not personality types, and cues can guide attention before scrutiny begins.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: What two conditions increase central processing?
cards.answer: Motivation to think about the issue and ability to do so, including time, attention and relevant knowledge.

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: Why is a cue not proof?
cards.answer: Authority, familiarity or consensus can guide judgement, but their relevance and trustworthiness must still be checked against evidence.

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: What does persuasion knowledge do?
cards.answer: It lets a recipient infer that someone is trying to influence them, identify tactics and adjust trust, attention or resistance.

cards.name: How does the mind process a pitch?
cards.q: A safari lodge asks why your redesign is worth USD 400 a month. What do you send?
cards.answer: Use two layers. First, give a one-sentence outcome hypothesis tied to its booking path. Then offer a short before-and-after audit, a named metric to test and a permissioned case study. Do not lean on polished visuals alone. Ask what evidence the owner needs to decide, then make that evidence easy to inspect and easy to reject.

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: True or false: the best seller is the most extroverted person in the room.
cards.answer: False. Grant's 2013 study of 340 representatives found an inverted-U relationship, with ambiverts outperforming extreme introverts and extroverts in that sample.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: Should you force a 43:57 talk-to-listen ratio on every call?
cards.answer: No. It is vendor data from Gong, not a law. Discovery needs listening; a technical demo or negotiation legitimately needs more seller explanation.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: In 60 words: what does consultative selling add?
cards.answer: Consultative selling treats the call as diagnosis and joint decision-making. The seller learns the current state, identifies a real problem, tests implications, understands desired outcomes and only then recommends a fit. Adaptiveness means changing the conversation to the buyer rather than reciting a script. It still requires a clear price and next step, without manufactured pressure.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: What four SPIN question types are used?
cards.answer: Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff.

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: What did Grant find?
cards.answer: In a sample of 340 outbound representatives, sales performance showed an inverted-U relationship with extraversion, with ambiverts performing better than extremes.

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: Why is the 43:57 ratio not a rule?
cards.answer: It is a Gong vendor benchmark from a selected conversation dataset, and the right mix varies by discovery, demo, technical explanation and negotiation.

cards.name: What do top sellers actually do differently?
cards.q: A dental clinic says its receptionist misses WhatsApp enquiries. How should you run discovery?
cards.answer: Ask what happens now, where enquiries drop, how many are missed, what a missed appointment is worth, who handles handoff and what a safe pilot would require. Summarise the clinic's words, verify the consequence, then propose a bounded automation with human escalation. Quote INR 20,000 with scope and exclusions, not a vague promise to increase revenue.

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: True or false: every loss is exactly twice as painful as the same gain is pleasurable.
cards.answer: False. The two-to-one slogan is not a universal constant. Gal and Rucker argued in 2018 that general loss aversion is often measurement-dependent, while other work finds robust effects in defined risky-choice and consumer contexts.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: If a default increases uptake, has the nudge definitely worked?
cards.answer: Not necessarily. Defaults can have real average effects, but nudge size varies by context and publication-bias correction. A live test needs a pre-specified outcome, opt-out visibility and null results.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the careful modern claim about loss aversion?
cards.answer: People often respond more strongly to losses than equivalent gains relative to a reference point, especially in specified decision contexts. But the size and presence of the effect depend on task, stakes, reference point and measurement. The two-to-one slogan is not a law. Use transparent framing, real costs and easy opt-out rather than manufactured fear.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: What does a reference point do?
cards.answer: It determines whether an outcome is experienced and described as a gain, loss or status quo change.

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: What did the nudge debate question?
cards.answer: Whether average effects remain substantial after correcting for publication bias, and whether one pooled effect generalises across contexts.

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: What is an ethical default?
cards.answer: A transparent, reversible choice architecture with an easy opt-out, disclosed interests and evidence from the actual setting.

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: A lodge owner fears losing high-season bookings and is considering your USD 500 retainer. How do you frame it?
cards.answer: Do not say the lodge will lose a guaranteed amount. Show the current enquiry-to-booking baseline, the assumptions behind a plausible improvement, the retainer cost, a bounded pilot and the stop rule. Present both the upside and the downside. A real capacity or deadline can be stated, but never use a fake countdown or hidden renewal.

cards.name: Why do losses loom larger than gains?
cards.q: A safari lodge owner says, "Your USD 400 monthly retainer sounds expensive. Another agency promises the same thing for USD 150, and I do not want a fake countdown." Give a response that transfers Week 1, not a pressure script.
cards.answer: First acknowledge the comparison and refuse fake urgency. Ask what outcomes, scope, response time, booking path and proof the USD 150 offer includes. Establish the lodge's current baseline and decision criteria before arguing price. Then state your bounded scope, assumptions, exclusions and a testable pilot, with a real stop date only if capacity genuinely requires it. Show one relevant case or audit, disclose uncertainty, and let the owner choose between a viable smaller scope, the proposed retainer or no deal. The honest levers are clarity, proof, real scarcity and real social proof, not fear.

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: True or false: a niche means refusing every customer outside one narrow industry.
cards.answer: False. A niche is a focused hypothesis about where fit and learning are strongest. You can accept exceptions, but your message, proof and prospecting should start where the pattern is clearest.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: Is “small business owner aged 30 to 50” an ideal customer profile?
cards.answer: Not by itself. It is a demographic description. An ICP should also name the job, trigger, current alternative, ability to pay, access and evidence of urgency.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is an ICP, and why is it not just a demographic segment?
cards.answer: An ideal customer profile is a testable account hypothesis. It names the situation, job, pain, alternative, trigger, ability to pay, access and decision context in which your offer should fit unusually well. Demographics can help locate people, but they do not explain value. The profile earns confidence only through conversations, trials, referrals and payment.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: What is the difference between a feature and a job?
cards.answer: A feature is something a product does. A job is the progress a buyer is trying to make in a situation, such as recovering missed enquiries without adding staff.

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: Why can a niche fail?
cards.answer: It may be too small, unreachable, unable to pay, or not united by a real problem. A narrow label is not evidence of demand.

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: What should you compare when positioning?
cards.answer: The buyer, their current alternative, the unique capability, the outcome it creates and the proof that the outcome is real.

cards.name: Who should you sell to?
cards.q: You want one message for every safari lodge, dental clinic and AI lead. How should you narrow the first test?
cards.answer: Run separate hypotheses. For safari lodges, test a mobile enquiry-to-booking audit for international guests. For clinics, test missed-call and WhatsApp response recovery. Track the same path from observation to reply, meeting, paid diagnostic and result. Keep the broader studio, but let each segment see a specific job, proof asset and next step.

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: True or false: a more emotional message is automatically more memorable and persuasive.
cards.answer: False. Emotion can help attention and memory, but truth, relevance, audience knowledge and a clear action still matter. A vivid false claim is memorable misinformation, not good communication.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: If a listener misunderstands a technical message, is the problem always their attention span?
cards.answer: No. The sender may be relying on knowledge the listener does not share. Newton’s tapper result is a warning to translate, exemplify and check understanding.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: In 60 words: how should a founder use the curse of knowledge?
cards.answer: Assume fluency is a sender-side illusion. Replace internal labels with an observable scene, a concrete outcome, a comparison the buyer recognises and one clear next step. Then ask the buyer to paraphrase the proposal. If the message is memorable but cannot survive a fact check or a correction, it is not good persuasion; it is merely effective attention capture.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: What was Newton’s surprising number?
cards.answer: Tappers expected listeners to identify about half their songs, but listeners identified only 2.5 percent in the dissertation task.

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: What does “what is / what could be” do?
cards.answer: It gives an audience a truthful contrast between the current state and a possible future, then asks what action could bridge the gap.

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: Why are stories not enough?
cards.answer: Stories improve vividness and recall but do not provide prevalence, causal proof or permission to generalise beyond the case.

cards.name: What makes a message stick?
cards.q: Your DM says “We help eco brands unlock digital growth.” Make it clearer without making it longer.
cards.answer: Try: “I noticed your Instagram sends guests to a booking page with no local-language FAQ. I sketched one mobile fix that could reduce repeated questions. If useful, I can send the two-minute audit; if not, no reply needed.” It is concrete, relevant, inspectable and easy to decline, with no invented result.

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: True or false: “B2B” means cold email is exempt from all consent and privacy rules.
cards.answer: False. CAN-SPAM has no B2B exception. UK PECR treats corporate subscribers differently from sole traders, and data protection still applies. India’s telecom rules and platform policies add separate constraints.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: Is five or seven follow-ups a proven universal rule?
cards.answer: No. The popular 80 percent after five touches statistic traces to a tiny 1942 survey with unavailable method details. Follow up only with a reason, measure your segment and stop at a no or opt-out.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: In 60 words: what should a respectful outbound message do?
cards.answer: It should identify a real fit, use one accurate observation, state a useful hypothesis, make a small and specific ask, identify the sender and give an easy exit. The sender records the contact source, legal basis or permission where relevant, channel, response and opt-out. If there is no reply, silence is not consent and persistence is not relevance.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: What is wrong with the 80 percent after five touches claim?
cards.answer: Its trace leads to a tiny 1942 survey whose method and denominator are unavailable. It is not a modern universal statistic.

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: What changed in TRAI’s 2025 amendment?
cards.answer: Commercial calls from normal 10-digit numbers were restricted; 140 remains for promotional calls and 1600 is designated for transactional and service calls.

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: What is the UK PECR B2B distinction?
cards.answer: Corporate subscribers can generally receive unsolicited marketing email without consent, while sole traders and some partnerships are treated as individuals and generally require consent or soft opt-in.

cards.name: Why do cold DMs, emails and calls get ignored?
cards.q: Write the honest version of a clinic call and safari DM without making either a manipulative script.
cards.answer: Callers should identify MTRX and the commercial purpose, ask if the owner has one minute for a question about missed calls or WhatsApp enquiries, and stop on no. The DM should name one observed booking friction, offer a short audit, say there is no obligation to reply, and include a clear stop path. Both should log source, consent or basis, outcome and opt-out.

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: True or false: correcting a false claim usually makes people believe it more strongly.
cards.answer: False as a general law. Wood and Porter found no general backfire across four experiments. Corrections can be modest, identity-sensitive and incomplete, but “backfire is typical” is not supported.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: Does lowering resistance mean agreeing with every objection?
cards.answer: No. It means understanding the barrier, preserving agency and answering with evidence. You can validate a concern without accepting a false premise or promising an unsuitable service.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the ethical way to lower resistance?
cards.answer: Diagnose the barrier rather than overpowering it. Acknowledge the person’s concern, preserve a genuine exit, ask questions that let them state priorities, offer bounded choices and make uncertainty measurable through a reversible test. Show relevant evidence and its limits. The goal is informed agency. If the offer is wrong, the honest result is a clear no.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: What does reactance protect?
cards.answer: A person’s perceived freedom of choice when a message or situation threatens to remove or control it.

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: What did the Roozenbeek field study measure?
cards.answer: Short prebunking videos improved recognition of manipulation tactics, confidence, trust discrimination and sharing decisions across a field study with 22,632 YouTube users.

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: Why is the backfire effect not a general law?
cards.answer: Wood and Porter found no general backfire across four experiments. Corrections can still be modest or moderated by identity, repetition and source trust.

cards.name: Why do people resist, and how do you lower the wall?
cards.q: A clinic owner says, “We already have a receptionist and I do not want a bot talking to patients.” How should you respond?
cards.answer: Do not argue that the owner is behind the times. Ask what the receptionist currently handles, where delays happen and what must remain human. Offer a bounded comparison, such as routing after hours or answering only agreed FAQs, with a human handoff, a success metric and an exit date. If that does not protect the clinic’s priorities, do not sell it.

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: True or false: asking a clinic owner whether they would buy an AI receptionist is strong evidence of demand.
cards.answer: False. It is a prediction, often shaped by politeness or the pitch. Ask about the last real enquiry, the current workaround and what they already paid to fix it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: Should every discovery call follow SPIN in exactly the same order?
cards.answer: No. SPIN is a useful observation-based framework, not a ritual. Start with the buyer's language and use only the questions needed to understand fit and consequence.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes a discovery question useful?
cards.answer: A useful question asks for observable behaviour, not applause for a proposed solution. Start with a recent event, reconstruct the process, find the hardest point, ask why it mattered, and learn the workaround. Then test the desired outcome and decision constraint. The buyer supplies evidence; the seller supplies attention, structure and an honest fit check.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: What are SPIN's four question types?
cards.answer: Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff. They are a sequence for diagnosing a problem, not mandatory wording.

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: Why is tell me about the last time stronger than would you buy?
cards.answer: A recent event contains behaviour, context and workaround evidence. A hypothetical answer is easily shaped by politeness, imagination or the seller's pitch.

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: What did the listening experiments find?
cards.answer: Across five experiments, high-quality listening increased attitude clarity, but not attitude correctness or intention to persuade.

cards.name: How do you ask questions without interrogating?
cards.q: A dental clinic owner says patients often miss appointments and asks for an AI reminder bot. What do you ask first?
cards.answer: Ask about the last missed appointment: how it was booked, when reminders were sent, who handled the reply, what the clinic did next and what the missed slot cost. Then ask what they have already tried and who approves a change. Only demo reminders if the evidence points there, and define human handoff and data boundaries.

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: True or false: Mehrabian proved that words carry only 7 percent of meaning in every conversation.
cards.answer: False. His studies used narrow, inconsistent messages about feelings and attitudes. The percentages do not describe lectures, sales calls, technical explanations or ordinary communication.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: Does neural coupling mean a speaker can upload a memory into another brain?
cards.answer: No. Coupling is measured statistical alignment in brain activity during a task. It is associated with comprehension in these studies, not literal memory transfer or mind reading.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the honest lesson behind 7-38-55?
cards.answer: Nonverbal cues matter, especially when words, voice and face conflict about an attitude. But the 7-38-55 percentages came from narrow 1967 experiments, not from all communication. In a real sales conversation, content, context, relationship, delivery and evidence interact. The practical lesson is to make signals consistent and check understanding instead of guessing from posture.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: What did Mehrabian actually measure?
cards.answer: Inference of positive or negative attitudes from brief, inconsistent combinations of words, vocal tone and facial expression, not the meaning of every message.

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: What did Hasson's coupling result predict?
cards.answer: Greater anticipatory speaker-listener coupling was associated with better comprehension in the fMRI story task.

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: What is the ethical use of mirroring?
cards.answer: Natural coordination and repeating language to check understanding, never theatrical copying of accent, identity or posture as a covert control tactic.

cards.name: What happens in two brains that are really communicating?
cards.q: You are showing a safari lodge owner a mobile booking flow and they go quiet. What do you do?
cards.answer: Do not infer rejection from body language or invoke 7-38-55. Pause, summarise the exact outcome and ask which part is unclear, risky or irrelevant. Invite them to walk through their current booking path. Then restate the next step in their language and ask them to correct your account before discussing price.

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: True or false: a warm, enthusiastic contact is automatically a champion.
cards.answer: False. A champion takes useful action, knows the internal process, has a reason to win and can help you reach the people who decide.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: Should you force every $300 to $500 lodge retainer through full enterprise MEDDPICC?
cards.answer: No. Use a light fit check for a small, owner-led deal. Reserve the full checklist for genuinely complex, multi-stakeholder decisions where paper, criteria and approval paths matter.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is a champion, and how do you test one?
cards.answer: A champion is not merely friendly. They have a personal reason to solve the problem, influence or access inside the buying group, knowledge of criteria and process, and willingness to take useful action. Test gently: ask for an internal introduction, a decision criterion, a shared document or a dated next step. If action never follows, downgrade the forecast.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: Why can the founder be the early product?
cards.answer: When software or proof is unproven, early buyers may be buying access to the founder's specific insight, judgement and ability to learn alongside them.

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: What six buying jobs did the Gartner report identify?
cards.answer: Problem identification, solution exploration, requirements building, supplier selection, validation and consensus creation.

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: What is the smallest honest qualification record?
cards.answer: Observed problem and impact, fit and constraints, decision people, timing, evidence needed, next action and owner.

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: Your two callers book a clinic meeting because the receptionist says the idea sounds interesting. What do you do before forecasting it?
cards.answer: Check whether the clinic has a real enquiry or follow-up problem, whether the owner or authorised manager will attend, what has already been tried, what outcome matters, whether healthcare data and handoff constraints are safe, and when a decision could happen. If the receptionist cannot open that path, label it an exploratory conversation, not a qualified opportunity.

cards.name: Who is worth pursuing?
cards.q: A safari lodge owner says: We want more direct bookings, your founder seems credible, and send a proposal for the full website and AI package. You have one 30-minute call left before they compare three agencies. What do you ask, what do you show, and what would make you walk away?
cards.answer: I would not treat enthusiasm as qualification. I would ask for a recent booking journey from Instagram to confirmation, where visitors drop out, what the lodge has already tried, the value of a direct booking, the seasonal constraint, the owner and operational stakeholders, the decision criteria, the alternative agencies, data and integration boundaries, and the date of the next decision. I would reflect the current state and ask what I misunderstood.I would show only the smallest relevant proof, such as a measured mobile booking friction and a short corrected flow, with evidence and limitations. I would offer a bounded audit or pilot and a mutual action plan with owners and dates. I would walk away, or close the loop, if the problem is not real, the buyer will not share the decision path, the requested claims exceed our evidence, the data handling is unsafe, or no one will take the next action. Credibility is useful only when the buying process can test it.

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: True or false: the 22 times figure is a settled result from Jerome Bruner's book.
cards.answer: False. The number is widely attributed to Bruner or Aaker, but no primary experiment supporting that exact ratio has been located. Keep the mechanism, drop the fake precision.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: If one lodge website case study doubled enquiries, does that prove a redesign will double every lodge's enquiries?
cards.answer: No. It is evidence that the change may work in a similar context, not a population estimate. State the baseline, comparison, time window and what remains unknown.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: In 60 words: why is the 22 times claim unsafe but storytelling still useful?
cards.answer: The exact 22 times ratio has no traceable primary study, so it should not be repeated as a law. Narrative transportation has experimental support: absorption can increase story-consistent beliefs and reduce counterarguing. Use a true, bounded case to make a problem imaginable, then add base rates, comparison data, limitations and a testable next step.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: What is narrative transportation?
cards.answer: Absorption in a story through attention, imagery and feeling. It can increase story-consistent beliefs, so it can carry error as well as truth.

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: What is the identifiable victim effect?
cards.answer: A named or pictured person can evoke more concern than an equivalent statistical group. It helps attention but can distort proportional judgement.

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: What should a B2B case study include?
cards.answer: Context and baseline, the intervention, a measured result with time window, permission, limitations and a clear statement of what it does not prove.

cards.name: Why do stories beat statistics, and when do they not?
cards.q: A safari lodge asks HansWild for a proposal because its Instagram posts receive attention but direct enquiries are weak. What do you send?
cards.answer: Open with one real guest journey, not a fabricated hero story. Show the exact mobile path and friction, then give the baseline enquiry data, a proposed change, a bounded pilot, expected indicators and risks. Keep the story for attention and empathy, and let the numbers decide whether the pilot worked.

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: True or false: showing more features makes a demo more persuasive.
cards.answer: False. More features can increase cognitive load. Start with the agreed job, show the shortest path to the outcome and name what is outside scope.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: Is a testimonial proof that the same result is guaranteed for a new client?
cards.answer: No. It is social evidence from one context. Pair it with the client type, baseline, time window, what changed and what remains uncertain.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes a demo persuasive without hype?
cards.answer: A persuasive demo begins with a diagnosed current state and a buyer-owned outcome. It shows the shortest path to that outcome, uses permissioned proof with a baseline and time window, names dependencies and exclusions, and leaves a reversible next step. It does not imply that one case guarantees the result for a different client.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: What is the feature to outcome chain?
cards.answer: A feature is a property, a capability is what it enables, and an outcome is the buyer-valued change. The chain must be explicit.

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: What belongs in a case study?
cards.answer: Context, baseline, intervention, measured result, time window, permission and limitations. A testimonial alone is not a causal estimate.

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: What is an honest risk reversal?
cards.answer: A bounded term that reduces uncertainty, such as a paid diagnostic credited to implementation or a defined pilot with a stop point, without claiming zero risk.

cards.name: How do you show value without hype?
cards.q: A dental clinic asks why MTRX should charge INR 20,000 for a WhatsApp automation when a cheaper plug-in exists. How do you present it?
cards.answer: Ask about missed enquiries and staff handoff first. Demo the exact patient question, routing and human escalation. Show the measured problem if available, state integration and support limits, compare total scope rather than only licence price, and offer a bounded pilot or decline if the clinic cannot resource follow-through.

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: True or false: a higher price always improves perceived and actual performance.
cards.answer: False. Price can shape expectations and sometimes experience, but effects depend on product, buyer knowledge, credibility and the task. Higher price can also trigger suspicion or reduce fit.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: If reframing changes perception, is the new value fake?
cards.answer: Not necessarily. Context, clarity, reassurance and service can create real utility. But a frame must not hide defects, costs, uncertainty or a weak result.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: In 60 words: what can price and framing legitimately do?
cards.answer: Price and framing can change reference points, expectations, confidence and the meaning of a service. Those effects can create real utility when they clarify quality, reduce uncertainty or improve the experience. They cannot excuse hidden costs, fake scarcity or unsupported promises. Because evidence is contextual, test the frame against a measured outcome and disclose the comparison.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: What did the 2005 placebo-price paper actually test?
cards.answer: Three experiments in which price cues around an energy drink were associated with puzzle performance, with the same product presented as discounted or regular price. It was not a universal premium law.

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: What happened in the Ariely data controversy?
cards.answer: Data Colada alleged fabricated data in a 2012 dishonesty field experiment in 2021. The paper was retracted, NPR reported insurer contradictions in 2023, and Duke's 2024 statement found no evidence Ariely knowingly falsified data but faulted safeguards.

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: What is a costly signal?
cards.answer: A cue that is credible partly because it is difficult or expensive to fake. It works only if the cost and the claimed quality are genuinely connected.

cards.name: Why is value in the eye of the beholder?
cards.q: A safari operator says a new website must look “luxury” so it can charge more, but has no new service evidence. What do you advise?
cards.answer: Do not sell luxury as a colour palette. Define the guest outcome and the operational proof: guide expertise, response time, conservation practice, room quality, transfer reliability and booking support. Build a visual frame that makes those real differences legible, then test qualified enquiries, conversion and guest feedback against the old experience.

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: True or false: every objection is a reflex that a skilled closer should overcome.
cards.answer: False. Some objections are conditions, some are misunderstandings and some are correct no-fit signals. Treating every no as resistance creates pressure and bad qualification.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: Does active listening mean staying silent and repeating the buyer's words?
cards.answer: No. Good listening includes attention, relevant questions, paraphrase when useful and a check that the concern was understood. It is active and two-way, not passive mimicry.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: In 60 words: how should a seller handle a price objection?
cards.answer: Pause and acknowledge that price matters. Ask what the buyer is comparing, what outcome would justify the investment and whether the issue is budget, scope, timing or risk. Explore before responding. Use a relevant baseline or case, state limits, offer a bounded alternative if it remains viable, check understanding and accept no when the fit is wrong.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: What can an objection be?
cards.answer: A condition, misunderstanding, missing stakeholder, lack of fit or polite exit. It is not automatically a reflex to overcome.

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: What is the listening loop?
cards.answer: Pause, acknowledge, clarify, explore, respond with relevant evidence or a clean no, then check whether the real concern was resolved.

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: Why are explicit objections not the whole story?
cards.answer: Real-call research found non-acceptances were often implicit and negotiated delicately. Hesitation, timing and attempts to end the interaction also carry information.

cards.name: What is an objection really telling you?
cards.q: A clinic owner says, “INR 15,000 is too much for a website,” then asks for a discount before discussing goals. What do you do?
cards.answer: Ask what they are comparing and whether the concern is cash this month, scope, trust or expected return. Ask how patients currently find and contact the clinic, show only the relevant path, define pages, revisions, hosting and support, and offer a smaller honest scope or a later date. If the economics do not work, thank them and stop.

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: True or false: the jam study proved that more options always reduce sales.
cards.answer: False. It was one field study. The 2010 meta-analysis found a mean effect near zero, with large variation by context and task.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: Should a studio offer one package only?
cards.answer: Not automatically. Offer a small, meaningful set when buyers differ, then make the differences concrete and easy to compare.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the modern lesson of the jam study?
cards.answer: The jam study shows that a large menu can attract attention while making purchase harder in one context. It does not show that more choice always hurts. A meta-analysis of 50 experiments found a mean effect near zero. Reduce comparison cost when options are complex, but preserve useful variety and test the whole funnel.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: What were the headline jam numbers?
cards.answer: About 60 percent stopped at 24 jams and 40 percent at 6; 3 percent of the large-display tasters bought versus 30 percent of the small-display tasters.

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: What did Scheibehenne et al. find?
cards.answer: Across 63 conditions from 50 experiments, N = 5,036, the mean choice-overload effect was d = 0.02, effectively zero.

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: When is a decoy ethically acceptable?
cards.answer: Only when the option represents a real, clearly described scope. A fake inferior option designed to steer a buyer is deceptive.

cards.name: Why does more choice sometimes kill the sale?
cards.q: A safari lodge asks for a website, booking-flow work and monthly content, but cannot compare six packages. What do you send?
cards.answer: Send three viable scopes, not six: a focused conversion site, a site plus booking and analytics work, and a seasonal growth retainer. State outcomes, response times, exclusions and a simple comparison. Ask which trade-off matters. Track proposal-to-close and delivery margin before deciding whether the menu is too large.

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: True or false: cost plus a margin is the fairest starting price for a studio.
cards.answer: False as a default. Cost is a sustainability floor; the buyer pays for a valuable, credible outcome. Use cost to reject unsustainable work, not to define value.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: Should you always quote in the buyer's currency?
cards.answer: Usually quote in the buyer's commercial currency when practical, but state tax, payment, exchange and scope terms clearly. Currency is not a substitute for value proof.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: In 60 words: how should you set a first service price?
cards.answer: Define the buyer, outcome, baseline and scope. Estimate willingness to pay from the value and alternatives, then check delivery cost, capacity and margin. Quote a clear range or three real packages, with payment and revision terms. Treat the first price as a testable hypothesis, not a secret discovered by arithmetic.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: What are the three YC pricing inputs?
cards.answer: A value equation, a cost floor and competition or alternatives, with the caveat that the talk is practitioner advice.

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: What should every MTRX concession buy?
cards.answer: A narrower scope, longer commitment, faster payment, access needed for delivery or permission to use a truthful case study.

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: Why can a cheap retainer be costly?
cards.answer: It can consume founder capacity, support time and cash-flow attention while leaving too little margin for delivery and learning.

cards.name: How do you price a service without guessing?
cards.q: Pitch one safari-lodge retainer and one Ahmedabad clinic package without pretending the prices are market facts.
cards.answer: For the lodge, propose $450 monthly for a defined three-month conversion retainer, tied to baseline and monthly tests. For the clinic, propose INR 15,000 for a fixed website, with INR 20,000 automation separately scoped. State exclusions and payment dates, ask the buyer to challenge the value equation, and log margin and close data.

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: True or false: closing means applying pressure until the buyer gives an answer.
cards.answer: False. A good close clarifies fit, authority, terms and the next decision. Pressure can create compliance without trust, fit or retention.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: If a buyer says they need to think, should you rebut immediately?
cards.answer: No. Ask what they need to evaluate, who else is involved and when a useful follow-up would be welcome. The answer may be a real condition, not resistance to overcome.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is an ethical close?
cards.answer: An ethical close makes the decision legible: fit, evidence, scope, price, authority and next date. It asks for a specific, proportionate commitment and leaves refusal safe. If a condition is missing, discover it or disqualify. Use real deadlines only, and never convert a buyer's uncertainty into a reason to hide information or apply pressure.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: What did SPIN change about closing?
cards.answer: It suggested that premature closing techniques can hurt larger sales by interrupting diagnosis and needs development.

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: What makes urgency honest?
cards.answer: A real, disclosed and verifiable start date, capacity limit, seasonal window or operational deadline.

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: What should a mutual action plan contain?
cards.answer: Tasks, owners, dates, decision authority, success criteria and a clear stop or revise point.

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: A lodge owner likes the proposal but says the board meets next Tuesday. What do you do?
cards.answer: Summarise the agreed problem, evidence, scope, price and open questions. Ask who must approve and what the board needs. Send a one-page proposal, agree a Tuesday follow-up, and make no claim that capacity expires before then. If the board says no, log the reason and leave the relationship intact.

cards.name: When should you ask for the decision?
cards.q: You have one week. Pitch one safari-lodge retainer abroad and one Ahmedabad clinic package, then ask for the decision without pressure. What do you say and what do you measure?
cards.answer: For the safari lodge, I would propose a three-month $450 monthly retainer with a defined conversion scope: one booking-flow or landing improvement monthly, two tested creative variants, analytics review and a short report. I would first ask for traffic, enquiry rate, average booking value, seasonality, decision authority and the lodge's alternative. I would label the expected uplift as a hypothesis, not a guarantee, and agree a baseline and review date.For the clinic, I would propose an INR 15,000 fixed website package with pages, copy responsibilities, two revision rounds and launch date stated. WhatsApp or AI receptionist automation would be a separate INR 20,000 package only after call volume, language, escalation, consent and support needs are known. I would trade concessions for narrower scope or faster payment, never discount without an exchange. I would end by asking whether the fit and terms support a start date, or whether we should stop. I would measure qualified replies, held calls, proposal-to-close, gross margin, days to payment, scope changes, retention and referrals by segment.

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: True or false: the first offer always wins the negotiation.
cards.answer: False. First offers often anchor, but information, alternatives, expertise and the bargaining context can reverse the advantage.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: A lodge wants a lower monthly fee. What should you calculate before replying?
cards.answer: Your target, your reservation price, your BATNA, and which scope or timing terms could be traded instead of simply discounting.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the ZOPA?
cards.answer: The zone of possible agreement is the overlap between the parties reservation limits. If a buyer can pay at most $450 and the seller will accept at least $400, the ZOPA is $400 to $450, assuming both limits are real. If there is no overlap, create value, improve alternatives, change scope, or walk away.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: What does BATNA protect you from?
cards.answer: It protects you from accepting a deal that is worse than a credible alternative. It also tells you where to invest before negotiating.

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: Why can logrolling create value?
cards.answer: Parties often value issues differently. One may care about price, the other about speed or access, so trading across issues can improve both outcomes.

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: What is the anchoring correction?
cards.answer: First offers can influence judgments, but the effect is context-dependent. Use a defensible, evidence-based number when you have enough information, and do not treat an arbitrary anchor as truth.

cards.name: How do you negotiate a deal?
cards.q: A safari lodge likes the redesign but asks for $300 per month instead of your $450 retainer. What do you do?
cards.answer: Ask what constraint the lower number represents, then compare it with your scope and BATNA. Offer a smaller, clearly named package at $300, or keep $450 for the original deliverables and trade a longer term, faster payment or permission to use a case study. If neither protects delivery quality, decline without drama.

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: True or false: a “no” means the buyer has rejected your value.
cards.answer: False. It may be a position protecting budget, status, timing, risk or a hidden alternative. Ask what the no is doing before trying to overcome it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: Does guanxi mean Chinese buyers simply prefer friends?
cards.answer: No. Research treats relationality as contextual and mixed with communication, power, face, credibility and information exchange, not as a cultural shortcut.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the honest use of tactical empathy?
cards.answer: Use it to test understanding, not to impersonate concern. Label a possible constraint, invite correction, and listen for interests behind the position. Then state your own limit and offer transparent options. The evidence supports perspective taking and some listening practices, but not a universal Voss script or a promise that tactical empathy beats alternatives.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: What does “go to the balcony” mean?
cards.answer: Pause and observe the negotiation from a wider perspective before reacting, keeping interests, relationship and future consequences visible.

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: What is the evidence status of Voss’s full package?
cards.answer: Partly supported at best. Related evidence favours perspective taking, but hostage-negotiation anecdotes do not establish causal business effects for the complete method.

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: Why is “Indian bargaining culture” a bad explanation?
cards.answer: Because market goods, uncertainty, relationships, language, status and institutions vary. Indian bazaar research is situated ethnography, not a claim about every Indian buyer.

cards.name: How do you negotiate when the other side has more power?
cards.q: A Marwari-owned clinic asks for a discount and says a cousin can build the site. How do you respond without stereotyping?
cards.answer: Ask what outcome, risk and timing the comparison represents. Explain your scope, evidence and walk-away floor, and offer a smaller package or a paid audit if that fits. Do not invoke community identity as proof of trust. Earn the relationship through clear work, references with permission and reliable follow-through.

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: True or false: a dark pattern is just an ugly website.
cards.answer: False. It is a choice architecture problem: deception, obstruction, hidden costs or pressure that undermines informed choice.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: What is the honest alternative to a fake countdown?
cards.answer: State a real deadline, its reason, the exact consequence, and what remains available after it. If nothing changes, do not invent urgency.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: In 60 words: how does inoculation help a buyer?
cards.answer: Inoculation gives a person a warning and a small, recognisable example of a tactic, then lets them practise refuting it. A buyer who knows to look for hidden fees, fake urgency or confirmshaming can pause and ask for the complete terms. It increases vigilance, not certainty, and works best with concrete, truthful examples.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: Name the 13 Indian CCPA patterns.
cards.answer: False urgency, basket sneaking, confirmshaming, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised advertisement, nagging, trick wording, SaaS billing and rogue malware.

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: What does the EU DSA Article 25 address?
cards.answer: Online platform interfaces that deceive, manipulate or materially distort a recipients ability to make free and informed decisions.

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: What is the honest replacement for high-pressure selling?
cards.answer: Visible identity, truthful claims, complete price, real evidence, real scarcity if any, an easy refusal and a clear exit path.

cards.name: How do you spot manipulation and defend against it?
cards.q: One caller says, “This offer expires today,” although MTRX can deliver the same clinic package next week. What do you change?
cards.answer: Remove the invented deadline. Give the caller an honest reason to call, a permission-based opening, the actual scope and price, and a follow-up date chosen by the clinic. Log the objection and opt-out. If a real capacity limit exists, state the number of available slots and what changes after they are filled.

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: True or false: a high NPS proves a client will renew.
cards.answer: False. NPS is a survey response, not a contract or causal guarantee. Track renewal, margin, outcomes and referrals alongside it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: What should a retainer promise?
cards.answer: A defined ongoing service, owner, response boundary, evidence of value, review rhythm and a clear way to change or end it.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: In 60 words: what should a monthly retention review contain?
cards.answer: Show the promised outcome, evidence delivered, unresolved risks, work completed, scope used, next decision and any change in price or responsibility. Compare with the client’s baseline, not just activity. Invite correction and make cancellation or reduction clear. A review is a joint decision about continued value, not a performance designed to prevent a no.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: What is NRR?
cards.answer: Starting recurring revenue plus expansion minus contraction and churn, divided by starting recurring revenue for the same cohort and time window.

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: What did the service-recovery meta-analysis find?
cards.answer: The paradox improved satisfaction on average, but not repurchase intentions, word of mouth or corporate image. It is not a reason to create failures.

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: Why does scope protect retention?
cards.answer: Clear scope prevents invisible work, surprise invoices and conflicting expectations. It lets a client choose an added service knowingly and lets the studio deliver the original promise well.

cards.name: What happens after the yes?
cards.q: A dental clinic on a INR 20,000 AI receptionist retainer keeps asking for new WhatsApp flows and says the old ones are “part of support.” What do you do?
cards.answer: Hold a review with the original scope, usage and outcome evidence. Separate bugs from new workflows, price the added work, and offer a revised tier if the need is recurring. Assign an owner and acceptance test for each flow. If the package no longer fits, make reducing or ending it straightforward and preserve the relationship.

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: True or false: if an AI message changes a belief, the persuasion was automatically good.
cards.answer: False. Accuracy, consent, disclosure, data use and harm still matter. A correct outcome does not excuse covert profiling or impersonation.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: Does personalisation always make a message more persuasive?
cards.answer: No. Effects depend on information quality, topic strength, interaction design and whether the model has a real reason to tailor the argument.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is the strongest evidence that AI can persuade?
cards.answer: Two controlled studies provide the clearest evidence. Costello, Pennycook and Rand found a roughly 20 percent reduction in conspiracy belief after personalised GPT-4 dialogue, persisting two months, among 2,190 Americans. Salvi and colleagues found higher odds of opinion movement when GPT-4 had basic demographic information. Neither study licenses covert profiling or proves general sales lift.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: What did the Science 2024 study find?
cards.answer: Among 2,190 Americans, personalised three-round GPT-4 dialogues reduced chosen conspiracy belief about 20 percent, lasting at least two months; sampled claims were 99.2 percent true.

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: What was Salvi et al.'s key number?
cards.answer: With personal information, GPT-4 debates had 81.2 percent higher odds of greater agreement than the human-human reference, N = 900, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 26.0 to 160.7 percent.

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: Why is the Zurich case not a clean experiment?
cards.answer: Participants were not informed, 34 accounts posted over 1,500 times using inferred sensitive traits and invented identities, and about half of AI-comment posts were deleted, undermining causal inference.

cards.name: Can AI persuade better than humans?
cards.q: You want an AI SDR to scan clinic websites and write highly personal Gujarati or Hindi calls. What is the ethical version?
cards.answer: Use only observable business facts, such as a broken booking form, and let a trained caller verify the observation. Identify MTRX, disclose meaningful automation where required, avoid patient or staff profiling, offer an easy opt-out, and audit held-meeting quality rather than maximising replies. AI may produce a draft; you own the evidence and the decision.

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: True or false: more activity automatically fixes a weak pipeline.
cards.answer: False. More activity can amplify poor fit, compliance risk and wasted follow-up. Improve definitions and conversion quality before increasing volume.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: Should you measure callers mainly by calls made?
cards.answer: No. Calls made are leading activity measures. Held, suitable meetings and downstream margin are outcome measures; use both and watch for gaming.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: In 60 words: what makes a sales process repeatable?
cards.answer: A repeatable process has a narrow fit hypothesis, defined stages, permissioned actions, clear owners, measurable conversion and a learning loop. It does not mean every buyer behaves identically. You should separate activity from outcomes, record losses and margin, test one cohort at a time, and revise the process when evidence or buyer feedback contradicts it.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: What is the difference between activity and outcome metrics?
cards.answer: Activity metrics count actions such as contacts or calls. Outcome metrics count what those actions produced, such as held qualified meetings, proposals, wins, margin and retention.

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: Give a usable MTRX pipeline.
cards.answer: Target account, permissioned contact, held discovery, qualified opportunity, proposal, signed SOW, first payment, retained month two, then referral or expansion.

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: Why can CAC and LTV mislead a studio?
cards.answer: CAC omits founder time, caller commissions or onboarding if defined narrowly; LTV becomes fantasy if it ignores gross margin, observed retention, churn and the time horizon.

cards.name: How do you build a repeatable founder sales system?
cards.q: How should you manage your two commission-only callers next month?
cards.answer: Define the ICP and compliant contact rule, give each caller the same short qualification form, and pay for held suitable meetings with a quality adjustment rather than raw bookings. Track contacts, replies, held meetings, qualification, proposals, wins, opt-outs and reasons lost. Review five calls weekly, update the Gujarati or Hindi wording from real objections, and stop any promise you cannot deliver.

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: True or false: ethical persuasion means avoiding emotion and influence entirely.
cards.answer: False. Clarity, stories, proof and appropriate emotion can help a person decide. Ethics constrains deception, coercion, exploitation and hidden pressure, not communication itself.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: Is social proof ethical whenever a real customer exists?
cards.answer: No. Get permission, represent the evidence accurately, disclose limits and never imply that one customer proves a universal result.
cards.label: Guess first

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: In 60 words: what is ethical persuasion?
cards.answer: Ethical persuasion helps another person understand a truthful option and choose freely. It can use clarity, proof, emotion, real scarcity and real social proof, but it does not hide material conditions, fabricate consensus, exploit vulnerability or punish refusal. You should disclose uncertainty, make exit easy, protect data, and review your code against every real deal.
cards.label: Explain it, video closed

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: What is the difference between detecting and fabricating influence?
cards.answer: Detecting makes a real condition visible, such as actual capacity or permissioned proof. Fabricating invents urgency, authority, consensus or obligation to steer a choice.

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: What does the Kantian test ask?
cards.answer: Whether you treat the buyer as a person with informed agency, or merely as a means to revenue. A useful counterfactual is whether you would disclose the tactic before the decision.

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: What does satyagraha add to a sales ethic?
cards.answer: A model of persuasion grounded in truth, self-restraint, nonviolence and willingness to bear costs oneself rather than impose hidden pressure on the other person.

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: Write three lines of your persuasion code for a safari lodge proposal.
cards.answer: I will show only permissioned proof and label estimates as estimates. I will state the complete scope, price, capacity limit and cancellation terms, and I will not invent a deadline. I will make a no or not-yet easy, record what I learned, and recommend another provider when MTRX is not the fit.

cards.name: What kind of persuader will you be?
cards.q: Can you take one realistic MTRX deal from first message to signed retainer and referral while using at least one idea from each week?
cards.answer: Model answer. You choose a Kenyan eco-lodge with an active Instagram account and a public mobile booking path that is slow and confusing. Week 1: you separate persuasion from manipulation, state a truthful observation, and use ethos, logos and pathos without pretending to know the lodge's revenue. Week 2: you send one relevant, permission-based DM, ask for a short discovery call, and use SPIN questions to learn direct-booking goals, seasonal constraints, decision makers and the cost of missed enquiries. You record the lodge's BATNA, including its current agency and doing nothing.Week 3: you reframe the offer around the lodge's desired outcome, show a permissioned before-and-after case with limits, and present good, better and best scopes. You anchor with a complete price, not a fake discount, then agree a paid audit or small pilot with a mutual action plan. Week 4: you trade scope, speed and support rather than silently conceding work; answer objections by clarifying conditions; write onboarding, analytics and cancellation terms; and set a real capacity limit based on your delivery calendar. If AI helped draft the message, you remain accountable and do not infer private staff or guest data.The lodge signs a three-month $400 monthly retainer with a defined mobile enquiry flow, analytics, two revision rounds and response times. You baseline enquiry clicks and completion before work, report what changed, and say what cannot yet be attributed. After a useful first month, you ask whether the owner would introduce one neighbouring lodge, make the referral request optional and supply a factual one-sentence description. The referral is earned social proof, not manufactured consensus. The deal is persuasive because the buyer can inspect the claim, compare alternatives, decline without punishment and still receive respect.
